Prodigal

PRAH-dih-gul -- from Latin prodigere ('to drive away, squander') -- not related to "prodigy" (Latin prodigium, 'an omen'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

To be prodigal is to be recklessly wasteful, squandering money or resources.

The prodigal heir burned through his entire inheritance on yachts and parties within eighteen months.

Worked Example

Long known in his hometown as the prodigal son who'd wasted his father's savings on foolish investments, he returned twenty years later with nothing but an apology.

Prodigal specifically describes wasteful spending or extravagance -- someone giving away or squandering resources recklessly, not someone talented or gifted (that would be a "prodigy," an entirely different word).

How Prodigal Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

wasteful

wasteful: using more of something than is needed, without care

extravagant

extravagant: spending far more than is reasonable or necessary

Antonyms

thrifty

thrifty: careful with money; not wasteful

sparing

sparing: using or spending very little

How Strong Is It? — lavish → prodigal → reckless

lavish vs. prodigal

lavish vs. prodigal: Lavish describes spending generously and richly, often in a positive light -- a lavish wedding.

reckless vs. prodigal

reckless vs. prodigal: Reckless goes further than prodigal, implying spending with no thought for consequences at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — prodig-

root — prodig-: to drive away, squander (Latin prodigere -- unrelated to 'prodigy')

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: having the qualities of; pertaining to

Put it together

Put it together: Prodigal comes from Latin prodigere, 'to drive away or squander,' plus -al. Despite its similar spelling, prodigal is not related to prodigy (Latin prodigium, 'an omen') -- a prodigal person wastes resources; a prodigy is simply a gifted young person.

Watch This Trap: Prodigal vs. Prodigy

Watch This Trap: Prodigal vs. Prodigy: Prodigal describes wasteful, extravagant spending -- the opposite of what its lookalike 'prodigy' (a young genius) might suggest. Don't confuse the two: a prodigal grandson wastes his fortune; a prodigy grandson might be a piano prodigy at age seven.
